title: The last line of this video might be the most cursed sentence I’ve ev...
transcript: when some Broadway audiences complained about the changed ending to the my Fair Lady revival many of them didn't realize the hilarious irony of how history was repeating itself welcome to another episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwback where I do retrospectives on recent theatre history. in 2018 Lincoln Center produced a large scale Broadway revival of my Fair Lady directed by Bartlett Sher. it was the third in a series of Golden Age revivals directed by Bartlett Sher at Lincoln Center following South Pacific and the king and I both of which were praised for being fairly traditional while using careful casting and direction to subdue some of the racial stereotypes and heightened the thoughtful nuance and he took a similar approach to my Fair Lady like some clever bits of staging that highlight that this is Eliza's story more than Higgins’s like using the revolve almost like a tracking shot in film to pin our focus on Eliza. but that was not the choice that raised controversy. while he didn't necessarily change the dialogue or the lyrics he did make one significant staging choice that effectively changed the textual ending instead of leaving us with the implication that Eliza returns to Higgins she defiantly leaps off the stage runs up the aisle and out the auditorium doors. both literally and symbolically depicting her rejection of Higgins in this moment of self-actualization naturally this provoked the ire of some musical theatre purists: how dare they change the ending to this classic musical? but the joke was on them because Barlett Sher is not the one who changed the ending to this story it was the writer of the musical Alan Jay Lerner. my Fair Lady is pretty closely based on George Bernard Shaw's 1912 play Pygmalion. but Shaw was ferociously adamant that Higgins and Eliza absolutely should not end up together. so much so that he wrote a 5,000 word essay to be included with the published script about why they're a terrible match. he maps out the entire trajectory of her relationship with Freddy. she takes business school classes to learn how to run a shop. there is also a weirdly long tangent about how Freddy's sister Clara becomes kind of a loser and gets really into HG Wells. as he maps out the rest of this story, Shaw admits that Eliza sometimes has fantasies of f**king Higgins but absolutely never wanted to marry him. not just because Higgins is an emotionally unavailable bully who's too in love with his mother to ever love a woman romantically but because Eliza is smart, perceptive, and self respecting enough to realize that. now some might respond to this by saying that while Pygmalion might work better with Shaw's ending that doesn't necessarily mean that my Fair Lady does. but I don't necessarily agree. my Fair Lady isn't so heavily adapted from Pygmalion that Shaw's arguments can't still apply. the songs give it a more romantic feel but the characters’ behavior, traits, and desires remain pretty much intact. I was tempted to take these final moments to talk about why purists infuriate me — and they do. but I have to admit it is a little more complicated here cause while it's definitely ironic that someone would criticize Sher for taking a creative license that basically just undoes the previous creative license I can't really blame it all on the my Fair Lady purists when the same thing essentially happened to Pygmalion back in the day the whole reason Shaw felt compelled to write that essay in the first place is because he was receiving so much pushback. some early productions even changed the ending without his permission all because shipping Dooliggins has been an extremely popular headcanon since the play's premiere
